summary: This is a Docker Compose configuration file that defines a development container service named 'quarto-doc-base'. It builds a Docker image from a local Dockerfile with customizable options for installing various tools, then runs the container with a specific user, working directory, mounted volumes for code and configuration, and a command that keeps it running indefinitely.

explanations.2: This is a spell-checker directive telling the tool to ignore the word 'tinytex' (probably a LaTeX distribution name) when checking this file.
explanations.6: This names the Docker image that will be created or used by this service.
explanations.8: The 'build' section tells Docker Compose how to build the image from scratch instead of pulling a pre-made one.
explanations.9: The context is the folder where Docker will find the Dockerfile and any files it needs to copy into the image.
explanations.11: These 'args' are variables passed to the Dockerfile during the build process to customize what gets installed.
explanations.15: UID (user ID) and GID (group ID) are set to 1000 as defaults, but VS Code will override these at runtime to match your actual user.
explanations.23: This sets which user account the container will run as; 'vscode' is a special user created by VS Code Dev Containers.
explanations.25: This sets the default directory the container opens to when you start working in it.
explanations.28: This mounts your project folder (parent directory) into the container at /workspace so changes on your computer are reflected inside the container.
explanations.29: This volume preserves your bash command history across container restarts by storing it in a local file.
explanations.30: This is an explicit 'bind mount' syntax that does the same thing as the simpler volume syntax above, but with more control.
explanations.31: The ${HOME} variable expands to your home directory path on your actual computer, so your Quarto configuration travels into the container.
explanations.34: This mounts your SSH private key into the container so it can authenticate with Git or other services using your credentials.
explanations.36: The 'read_only' flag means the container can read your SSH key but cannot modify it, which is a security best practice.
explanations.39: This command runs an infinite loop that sleeps, effectively keeping the container running so you can connect to it and use it as needed.
